Connection Title: The four defects in tetralogy of Fallot
Explanation: These are the four defining abnormalities of tetralogy of Fallot. The degree of pulmonary outflow obstruction determines much of its shunt physiology.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tetralogy of Fallot; TOF components
Source Section: Cyanotic Congenital Heart Defects / Tetralogy of Fallot, PDF p.166
Notes: All four are the defining components of TOF (infundibular/pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD, RVH). Clean defining-set; no equally strong competing category.

Connection Title: Classic causes of high-output heart failure
Explanation: Each can create a high-output state that becomes heart failure when cardiac output cannot meet the increased demand or low-resistance circulation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: High-output HF causes; High-output cardiac failure
Source Section: Heart Failure / High and Low Output Heart Failure, PDF p.123
Notes: All four confirmed high-output HF causes (Bozkurt, Universal Definition of HF, J Card Fail 2021; Reddy, High-Output HF 15-Year Experience, JACC 2016). Qualify anemia as severe and fistula as hemodynamically significant; none invariably causes HF. 'High-output states' is a broader alias. Board overlap: AV fistula hemodynamics resemble CARD-052.

Explanation: All inhibit vascular L-type calcium channels and primarily reduce arterial resistance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: DHP calcium channel blockers; Vascular calcium channel blockers
Source Section: Vasodilation and Vasoconstriction / Pharmacologic Targets, PDF p.57
Notes: All four are dihydropyridines (Abernethy & Schwartz, Calcium-Antagonist Drugs, NEJM 1999). Clean, unambiguous class set.

Explanation: These agents preferentially antagonize beta-1 receptors. The source links renal beta-1 blockade to reduced renin release.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cardioselective beta blockers; Selective beta-1 antagonists
Source Section: RAAS / Direct Pharmacologic Targets, PDF p.77
Notes: All four are beta-1 selective (Joseph et al, JACC 2019; AlHabeeb, Cardiovasc Drugs Ther 2022). Selectivity is relative and lost at high dose; nebivolol is third-generation with additional NO-mediated vasodilation but retains the highest beta-1 selectivity. Renin reduction via renal beta-1 blockade is valid.

Connection Title: Non-antiarrhythmic drugs that can prolong QT
Explanation: The source lists all four as potential acquired QT-prolonging exposures, which can increase torsades risk.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: QT-prolonging noncardiac drugs; Drugs associated with acquired long QT
Source Section: Cardiac Conductive Physiology / QT Interval Prolongation, PDF p.88
Notes: All four prolong QT (Tisdale, Drug-Induced Arrhythmias, Circulation 2020; FDA ziprasidone label). Ziprasidone is classified 'conditional risk' of TdP vs 'known risk' for the other three - the weakest but still valid member. Risk is dose/route/interaction dependent. Board overlap with CARD-006 (QT theme).

Explanation: The three class IA agents and sotalol are all listed as drugs that can prolong ventricular repolarization and QT.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics; Antiarrhythmics associated with torsades
Source Section: Cardiac Conductive Physiology / QT Prolongation, PDF p.88; Antiarrhythmics, PDF pp.92,94
Notes: All four prolong QT/cause TdP (Tisdale, Circulation 2020; FDA sotalol label). Sotalol is class III (with class II beta-blocking properties), NOT class IA - title correctly avoids 'class IA.' Three members are class IA (deliberate 3+1 overlap): when assembling a 16-tile board, do not also create a separate 'class IA' group.

Connection Title: Drugs that slow AV nodal conduction
Explanation: Each can slow transmission through the AV node. They do so through different mechanisms and may contribute to AV block.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: AV nodal blockers; Drugs that slow AV conduction
Source Section: Antiarrhythmics, PDF pp.93,95; Conduction Blocks, PDF p.114; Heart Failure / Digoxin, PDF p.124
Notes: All four slow AV nodal conduction (Tisdale, Circulation 2020; 2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline, Joglar, JACC 2024). Digoxin acts via increased vagal tone (not Ca/beta blockade). Accept 'AF rate-control drugs' as a clinical alias, but do not imply use in pre-excited AF, and note verapamil/diltiazem are contraindicated in HFrEF.

Explanation: The source associates amiodarone with pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic and pigment-related adverse effects.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Amiodarone adverse effects; Amiodarone toxicity
Source Section: Antiarrhythmics / Other Drug Properties and Adverse Effects, PDF p.97
Notes: All four are classic amiodarone toxicities (Zimetbaum, NEJM 2007; FDA amiodarone label; 2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline). Corneal microdeposits and photosensitivity are also common but not required for this set.

Connection Title: Important adverse effects of ACE inhibitors
Explanation: These are source-listed adverse effects or pregnancy-related hazards of ACE inhibition.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ACE inhibitor adverse effects; ACE inhibitor safety concerns
Source Section: Hypertension / Antihypertensives, PDF p.203
Notes: Cough, angioedema, and hyperkalemia are class adverse effects; fetal toxicity is a pregnancy-specific (2nd/3rd trimester) hazard rather than a routine adult symptom (2025 AHA/ACC HTN guideline, Jones, JACC 2025). The 'safety concerns' framing accommodates the mixed category.

Explanation: The source lists hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia and hyperglycemia among thiazide-associated adverse effects.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Thiazide adverse effects; Thiazide-associated laboratory abnormalities
Source Section: Hypertension / Thiazide Diuretics, PDF p.203
Notes: All four are recognized thiazide metabolic effects (2025 AHA/ACC HTN guideline, Jones, JACC 2025); hypercalcemia and dyslipidemia also occur. These are potential, not inevitable, changes.

Explanation: The source links these toxic, infectious and nutritional causes to ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: DCM causes; Causes of dilated systolic cardiomyopathy
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Dilated Cardiomyopathy, PDF p.128; Chagas Disease, PDF p.132
Notes: All four are recognized DCM causes; selenium deficiency = Keshan disease (Sliwa, JACC Focus Seminar 2022; Bozkurt, Current Diagnostic/Treatment Strategies for Specific DCM, Circulation 2016). Exposure/deficiency does not always produce DCM. Board overlap: shares doxorubicin and alcohol with CARD-054 - do not place both on the same 16-tile board.

Connection Title: Conditions that can produce restrictive cardiomyopathy
Explanation: These are grouped in the source as infiltrative or radiation-related causes of impaired ventricular filling.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Restrictive cardiomyopathy causes; Causes of restrictive myocardial filling
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, PDF p.129
Notes: All four are accepted restrictive cardiomyopathy causes (Pereira/Grogan/Dec, Spectrum of Restrictive and Infiltrative Cardiomyopathies, JACC 2018; Muchtar, Circ Res 2017). AMBIGUITY REVISED 2->1: the competing 'infiltrative cardiomyopathy' label fits only amyloid/hemochromatosis/sarcoidosis (NOT radiation), so it is not an equally strong category for the full four. Radiation is dual-pathology (restrictive CM + constrictive pericarditis) - board overlap with CARD-033; amyloid overlaps restrictive-physiology themes.

Connection Title: Classic features of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Explanation: These describe the characteristic structure, histology, obstruction and preload-sensitive murmur of HOCM.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: HOCM findings; Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy, PDF p.130
Notes: Verified: Valsalva (reduced preload) augments dynamic LVOT obstruction and murmur; asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte/myofibrillar disarray are characteristic (Veselka, Lancet 2017; Braunwald, HCM, NEJM 2025). Specify the obstructive phenotype and the strain phase of Valsalva.

Explanation: The source describes a stress-associated syndrome with transient ventricular dysfunction and a classic ballooning pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Stress cardiomyopathy; Broken-heart syndrome; Takotsubo clues
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy, PDF p.133
Notes: All four are classic Takotsubo features (Bozkurt, Circulation 2016; 2023 ESC Cardiomyopathies guideline, Arbelo). Apical ballooning is the most common (not the only) variant; these are associations, not diagnostic requirements.

Explanation: The source links this parasite and its insect vector to chronic cardiac and gastrointestinal disease, including esophageal and colonic dilation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Chagas associations; American trypanosomiasis
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Chagas Disease, PDF p.132
Notes: T. cruzi, the triatomine (reduviid) vector, and chronic GI mega-syndromes (megaesophagus, megacolon) are classic Chagas associations; cardiac/DCM link in Schultheiss, Dilated Cardiomyopathy, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019. GI mega-syndromes are standard chronic-Chagas teaching (original source supports the association). Cross-system (CV/GI) retained.

Explanation: The source links defective fibrillin to these characteristic ocular and cardiovascular findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Marfan findings; FBN1-related disease clues
Source Section: Aortic Disease / Marfan Syndrome, PDF p.143
Notes: FBN1 (fibrillin-1), ectopia lentis (classically superior/upward), aortic root dilation, and MVP are core Marfan features (Loeys et al, revised Ghent nosology for Marfan syndrome, J Med Genet 2010). Findings vary between patients; 'connective tissue disease' is too broad to be equally specific.

Explanation: These are source-listed anatomic and clinical clues to aortic coarctation, with collateral-related rib changes in established disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Coarctation findings; Aortic isthmus obstruction clues
Source Section: Aortic Disease / Aortic Coarctation, PDF p.144
Notes: Juxtaductal narrowing, radio-femoral delay, rib notching (intercostal collaterals), and claudication are classic (Brickner & Hillis, Congenital Heart Disease in Adults, NEJM 2000; Chen & Wei, Aortic Coarctation, NEJM 2024). Rib notching and claudication reflect established disease, not neonatal presentation.

Explanation: The three exertional symptoms form the classic symptomatic AS triad, and a small delayed pulse reflects impaired ventricular ejection.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Aortic stenosis clues; Symptomatic AS
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Aortic Stenosis, PDF p.148
Notes: Exertional dyspnea, angina, and syncope (classic AS triad) plus pulsus parvus et tardus (Otto, Calcific AS, JAMA 2024; Manning, JAMA 2013). Parvus et tardus may be absent in elderly stiff arteries; HOCM overlaps the exertional symptoms but the small/delayed pulse favors fixed AS. Group mixes symptoms and a sign.

Explanation: Chronic AR can produce a large systolic-diastolic pressure difference and peripheral pulsations alongside its characteristic diastolic murmur.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Chronic AR findings; Aortic insufficiency clues
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Aortic Regurgitation, PDF p.149
Notes: Wide pulse pressure, water-hammer/Corrigan pulse, de Musset head-bobbing, and early diastolic decrescendo murmur characterize chronic significant AR (Choudhry & Etchells, Does This Patient Have Aortic Regurgitation?, JAMA 1999). Peripheral signs are typical of chronic (not acute) AR; the murmur is auscultatory rather than strictly 'peripheral.'

Explanation: The source links obstructed mitral inflow to these auscultatory findings and left atrial enlargement.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mitral stenosis clues; Rheumatic mitral stenosis findings
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Mitral Stenosis, PDF p.150
Notes: Opening snap, loud S1, apical diastolic rumble, and LA enlargement are classic MS findings (Chandrashekhar, Mitral Stenosis, Lancet 2009; Carabello & Crawford, NEJM 1997). Loud S1 and OS require a pliable valve and may be lost with heavy calcification; the Austin Flint murmur of AR can mimic the rumble.

Explanation: Mitral regurgitation is associated with this murmur pattern, an acute post-infarct mechanism and elevated atrial systolic filling waves.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mitral regurgitation clues; Mitral insufficiency associations
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Mitral Regurgitation, PDF pp.151,154; Cardiac Cycle, PDF p.71
Notes: Apical holosystolic murmur radiating to axilla, papillary muscle rupture (acute post-MI mechanism), and a prominent LA v wave characterize MR (Damluji, Mechanical Complications of AMI, Circulation 2021; Carabello & Crawford, NEJM 1997). The v wave is left atrial, not jugular; a loud murmur may be absent in acute severe MR.

Tile 4: Tricuspid infection in injection drug use
Explanation: These findings and a classic infectious cause support tricuspid regurgitation and its right-sided venous congestion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tricuspid regurgitation clues; Tricuspid insufficiency associations
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Tricuspid Regurgitation, PDF p.153
Notes: LLSB holosystolic murmur, inspiratory augmentation (Carvallo sign), elevated JVP, and IVDU-associated tricuspid endocarditis support TR (Carabello & Crawford, Valvular Heart Disease, NEJM 1997). IVDU is a risk context, not a universal cause; avoid building a separate tricuspid-endocarditis group on the same board.

Connection Title: Settings in which an S3 may be heard
Explanation: The source lists a physiologic S3 in pregnancy and pathologic S3 associations in volume-loaded or systolically failing ventricles.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: S3 associations; Third heart sound settings
Source Section: Cardiac Cycle / S3, PDF p.67
Notes: Physiologic S3 in pregnancy/young patients; pathologic S3 in systolic HF and significant chronic MR/AR (volume overload) (Sato, Third and Fourth Heart Sounds, Circ J 2018). Do not label all four as heart failure; regurgitation should be significant and usually chronic.

Explanation: Atrial contraction into a less compliant ventricle can produce S4 in these source-listed conditions.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: S4 associations; Fourth heart sound settings; Stiff-ventricle conditions
Source Section: Cardiac Cycle / S4, PDF p.67; Cardiomyopathy / HOCM, PDF p.130
Notes: S4 arises from atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle: chronic HTN, AS, HFpEF (diastolic HF), and HOCM (Vidt & Prisant, Hypertensive Heart Disease, J Clin Hypertens 2008; Adegunsoye, Echocardiography 2011; Sato, Circ J 2018). Requires effective atrial contraction (absent in AF). 'Impaired ventricular compliance' is an acceptable mechanistic alias.

Explanation: The source links persistent ductal patency to this murmur, runoff physiology and pharmacologic closure in selected premature infants.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PDA clues; Persistent ductus arteriosus
Source Section: Acyanotic Congenital Heart Defects / PDA, PDF p.161
Notes: Continuous (machinery) murmur, wide pulse pressure, aorta-to-PA shunt, and indomethacin-induced closure characterize PDA (May, The ductus arteriosus, Pediatr Radiol 2023). Left-to-right shunt describes the pre-Eisenmenger state; indomethacin applies to preterm infants, not all PDA.

Connection Title: Transposition of the great arteries clues
Explanation: The source describes discordant ventricular-arterial connections creating parallel circuits, with this classic radiographic appearance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: TGA findings; D-transposition of the great arteries
Source Section: Cyanotic Congenital Heart Defects / Transposition, PDF p.167
Notes: Parallel circulations, ventriculoarterial discordance (RV->aorta, LV->PA), and the egg-on-a-string radiograph define D-TGA (Canan, Multimodality Imaging of TGA, Radiographics 2021; Ferguson, Classic Imaging Signs, Radiographics 2007). The radiographic sign may be absent on early neonatal films.

Explanation: Uncoordinated atrial activity explains absent organized atrial signals, irregular ventricular timing and the source-described pulmonary vein trigger sites.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: AF findings; Atrial fibrillation associations
Source Section: Atrial Arrhythmias / Atrial Fibrillation, PDF pp.101-103; Anatomy / Ablation, PDF p.16
Notes: Irregularly irregular R-R, absent discrete P waves, absent jugular a waves, and pulmonary-vein ostial triggers characterize AF (2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline, Joglar, JACC 2024; Ko, Atrial Fibrillation, JAMA 2025). ECG clues presume conducted AF (not a paced or complete-block rhythm).

Explanation: These source-described features link typical right atrial macro-reentrant flutter to its atrial waveform, common conduction ratio and ablation target.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Typical flutter; Cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent atrial flutter
Source Section: Atrial Arrhythmias / Atrial Flutter, PDF p.104; Anatomy / Ablation, PDF p.16
Notes: Sawtooth waves, right-atrial macro-reentry, common 2:1 AV conduction, and CTI ablation target define typical (CTI-dependent) atrial flutter (2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline, Page; 2023 ACC/AHA AF guideline). Qualify as typical flutter; atypical flutter uses other circuits and conduction need not be 2:1.

Explanation: An accessory atrioventricular pathway causes early ventricular activation and the source-listed sinus-rhythm pre-excitation pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: WPW pattern; Ventricular pre-excitation; Wolff-Parkinson-White findings
Source Section: Ventricular Arrhythmias / WPW, PDF p.109
Notes: Bundle of Kent (accessory pathway), short PR, delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), and wide QRS in sinus rhythm define the WPW pre-excitation pattern (Thakkar, JAMA Intern Med 2021; Brady, 2023). Applies to sinus-rhythm pre-excitation; orthodromic AVRT is narrow-complex.

Explanation: Pericardial inflammation produces this characteristic positional pain, rub and ECG pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acute pericarditis clues; Pericardial inflammation findings
Source Section: Pericardial Disease / Acute Pericarditis, PDF p.206
Notes: Positional (leaning-forward) relief, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation, and PR depression are classic acute pericarditis findings (Imazio, Evaluation and Treatment of Pericarditis, JAMA 2015; 2025 ACC pericarditis consensus, Wang). Not all are present in every case; early repolarization can mimic the ST changes.

Explanation: The source links impaired filling from a rigid pericardium to these findings, including accelerated early venous emptying before filling is abruptly limited.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pericardial constriction findings; Constrictive physiology clues
Source Section: Pericardial Disease / Constrictive Pericarditis, PDF p.207; Cardiac Cycle / Jugular Waveform, PDF p.70
Notes: Pericardial knock, Kussmaul sign, pericardial calcification, and rapid y descent indicate constrictive pericarditis (Geske, Differentiation of Constriction and Restriction, JACC 2016; 2025 ACC pericarditis consensus). Kussmaul sign and rapid y descent overlap with restrictive cardiomyopathy (board overlap with CARD-012) - calcification and knock favor constriction; calcification present in only ~20-40%. Contrast y descent with CARD-034 (blunted in tamponade).

Explanation: The first three are Beck-triad findings; exaggerated inspiratory systolic pressure decline is another classic tamponade clue in the source.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tamponade clues; Beck triad plus pulsus paradoxus
Source Section: Pericardial Disease / Cardiac Tamponade, PDF p.209
Notes: Hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds (Beck triad) plus pulsus paradoxus characterize tamponade (Adler, Cardiac Tamponade, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2023; Chiabrando, JACC 2020). The full Beck triad is insensitive in slowly accumulating medical effusions; neck veins may be less prominent with hypovolemia. The y descent is blunted (contrast CARD-033).

Connection Title: Events that can cause cardiac tamponade
Explanation: The source lists dissection, myocardial rupture, trauma and postoperative complications as possible sources of a rapidly pressurized pericardial collection.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tamponade causes; Causes of pericardial compression
Source Section: Pericardial Disease / Cardiac Tamponade, PDF p.209
Notes: Aortic dissection (proximal), LV free-wall rupture, penetrating trauma, and cardiac surgery cause rapidly accumulating hemopericardium -> tamponade (2025 ACC pericarditis consensus, Wang; Damluji, Circulation 2021). Dissection must involve proximal anatomy. 'Hemopericardium causes' is an acceptable mechanistic alias.

Explanation: These infectious, metabolic, post-infarct immune and treatment-related processes can cause pericardial inflammation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pericarditis etiologies; Causes of pericardial inflammation
Source Section: Pericardial Disease / Acute Pericarditis, PDF p.206
Notes: Coxsackie B (viral), uremia (metabolic), Dressler syndrome (post-MI immune), and radiation are recognized pericarditis causes (Imazio, JAMA 2015; 2025 ACC pericarditis consensus etiology table, Wang). Irradiation causes several cardiac complications, pericarditis among them.

Explanation: Ventricular arrhythmia and the three mechanical ruptures (papillary muscle, interventricular septum, LV free wall) are recognized post-MI complications that occur on distinct timelines: arrhythmias may be early, whereas mechanical ruptures typically present about 3-5 days after a transmural infarct. The grouping does not imply a shared day of onset.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Post-MI complications; Complications after myocardial infarction
Source Section: Myocardial Infarction / Post-MI Timeline, PDF p.186
Notes: All four are verified MI complications (Damluji, Mechanical Complications of AMI, Circulation 2021; Murphy & Goldberg, Am J Med 2022). REVISION: explanation reworded to state distinct timelines and remove any implication of a shared onset day. Competing 'mechanical rupture' fits only 3 (not arrhythmia), so is not an equally strong category for the full four.

Connection Title: ECG leads viewing the lateral wall
Explanation: These are grouped in the source as lateral-wall leads used in infarct localization.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Lateral ECG leads; Lateral infarct lead territory
Source Section: Myocardial Infarction / ECG Localization, PDF pp.187-188
Notes: I, aVL, V5, and V6 are the lateral leads for infarct localization (Thygesen, Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction, JACC 2018). Clean, unambiguous territory set.

Connection Title: Precordial leads spanning the anterior-septal territory
Explanation: The source groups V1-V4 under anterior infarct localization, with V1-V2 more septal and V3-V4 more anterior/apical.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Anterior-septal ECG leads; Anterior infarct lead territory
Source Section: Myocardial Infarction / ECG Localization, PDF pp.187-188
Notes: V1-V4 span the anteroseptal territory (V1-V2 septal, V3-V4 anterior/apical) (Thygesen, Fourth Universal Definition of MI, JACC 2018). Territory labels vary by convention; do not infer a single culprit artery from each individual lead.

Connection Title: Drug exposures associated with coronary vasospasm
Explanation: The source lists these exposures as associations or precipitants of vasospastic angina.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Coronary vasospasm triggers; Drug-associated vasospastic angina
Source Section: Stable Angina and Atherosclerosis / Vasospastic Angina, PDF p.179
Notes: Cocaine, amphetamines, triptans (5-HT1B agonists), and ergot alkaloids can precipitate coronary vasospasm (Waterbury, Non-atherosclerotic causes of ACS, Nat Rev Cardiol 2020; FDA sumatriptan label). Clinical incidence with triptans is low; an exposure alone is not diagnostic of vasospasm. 'Vasoconstrictive substances' is a broader alias.

Connection Title: Signals recruiting smooth muscle cells into atheroma
Explanation: The source lists these signals in recruitment of vascular smooth muscle cells to the intima during atherosclerotic plaque development.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Smooth muscle recruitment signals in atherosclerosis; Intimal smooth muscle recruitment mediators
Source Section: Stable Angina and Atherosclerosis / Pathogenesis, PDF p.175
Notes: PDGF and FGF are direct VSMC mitogens/chemoattractants; endothelin-1 potentiates PDGF-driven migration and IL-1-beta drives phenotypic switching and upregulates PDGF receptors (Delafontaine, Growth Factors and VSMC Growth, Eur Heart J 1998; He, Nat Commun 2015; Chen, PNAS 2006). ET-1 and IL-1 act more indirectly - use 'atherosclerotic signaling mediators' as a broader alias. Hard difficulty appropriate.

Explanation: Failed venous valves and elevated venous hydrostatic pressure connect these source-listed findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Venous insufficiency clues; Chronic venous hypertension findings
Source Section: Peripheral Venous and Arterial Disease / Chronic Venous Insufficiency, PDF p.193
Notes: Varicose veins, hemosiderin (brown) ankle hyperpigmentation, duplex venous reflux, and elevation-responsive edema reflect chronic venous hypertension (Fukaya & Kolluri, Nonsurgical Management of CVI, NEJM 2024; Gloviczki, SVS/AVF guideline, J Vasc Surg 2011). Reflux on ultrasound is a diagnostic test rather than a bedside sign. 'Venous stasis disease' is an acceptable alias.

Explanation: These source-described findings indicate impaired lower-limb arterial perfusion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PAD findings; Lower-limb arterial insufficiency
Source Section: Peripheral Venous and Arterial Disease / PAD and ABI, PDF p.194
Notes: Claudication, diminished distal pulses, distal hair loss, and ABI <0.9 indicate PAD (2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline, Gornik, JACC 2024; Criqui, AHA Scientific Statement, Circulation 2021). Threshold is technically ABI <=0.90; noncompressible (calcified) vessels can falsely elevate ABI. 'Limb ischemia' is an acceptable broader alias.

Explanation: The source lists these endocrine disorders as underlying causes of secondary hypertension through different hormonal mechanisms.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hormonal causes of hypertension; Endocrine secondary hypertension
Source Section: Hypertension / Secondary Hypertension, PDF p.202
Notes: Cushing syndrome, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, and hyperthyroidism are endocrine causes of secondary hypertension; hyperthyroidism is explicitly listed in the 2025 AHA/ACC HTN guideline table (prevalence <1%) (Jones, JACC 2025; de Silva, Endocrine Causes of Hypertension, Curr Hypertens Rep 2020; Rivas, Am J Med Sci 2021). Hyperthyroidism often produces predominantly systolic HTN. Cross-system (CV/endocrine) retained.

Explanation: These source-listed causes can reduce effective circulating volume through blood or fluid losses.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hypovolemic shock causes; Severe circulating-volume loss
Source Section: Shock / Hypovolemic Shock, PDF p.213
Notes: Traumatic hemorrhage, upper GI bleeding, severe diarrhea, and major burns reduce effective circulating volume -> hypovolemic shock (Vincent & De Backer, Circulatory Shock, NEJM 2013). Losses must be substantial; burns combine fluid shifts with losses. 'Hemorrhagic shock' fits only the two bleeding causes, so is not an equally strong category for the full four.

Connection Title: Major components of the cardiac conduction pathway
Explanation: These source-listed structures initiate, delay and distribute the impulse through the heart. Bundle branches are intermediate components as well.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cardiac conduction structures; Specialized cardiac conduction system
Source Section: Anatomy / Cardiac Conduction, PDF p.15; Cardiac Conductive Physiology, PDF p.85
Notes: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje network are the major components of the specialized conduction system (Anderson, The anatomy of the cardiac conduction system, Clin Anat). This is a selection of major structures (bundle branches omitted), not an exhaustive list; no equally strong competing system.

Connection Title: The four phases of a ventricular pressure-volume loop
Explanation: These are the four source-listed phases of a ventricular pressure-volume loop under normal valve function.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PV loop phases; Four ventricular cycle phases
Source Section: Pressure Volume Loops / Basic Principles, PDF p.45
Notes: Isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, and filling are the four PV-loop phases under normal valve function (Hall, Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). Clean defining set.

Explanation: The source connects angiotensin II to increased vascular resistance and volume retention through these direct and endocrine actions.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Angiotensin II effects; AT-II actions
Source Section: RAAS / Actions of Angiotensin II, PDF p.75
Notes: Arteriolar constriction, increased proximal-tubule Na reabsorption, aldosterone release, and vasopressin release are direct and endocrine actions of angiotensin II (Turcu, Primary Aldosteronism, Nat Rev Endocrinol 2022; Hall, Angiotensin in Critical Care, Crit Care 2018). Actions occur across different tissues; 'RAAS activation' is a broader acceptable alias.

Explanation: The source describes PLC generating IP3 and DAG, with DAG activating PKC in the vascular Gq pathway.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Gq signaling cascade; PLC-IP3-DAG pathway
Source Section: Vasodilation and Vasoconstriction / Gq Pathway, PDF p.56
Notes: PLC generates IP3 and DAG; DAG activates PKC in the Gq vascular pathway (Webb, Smooth muscle contraction and relaxation, Adv Physiol Educ 2003). These are cascade components (not four receptors or four enzymes of one class); 'Gq-linked second-messenger signaling' is an equivalent alias. Hard difficulty appropriate.

Explanation: The source groups these under Reichert cartilage derivatives of the second pharyngeal arch.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Reichert cartilage derivatives; Second arch skeletal derivatives
Source Section: Embryology / Pharyngeal Arches table, PDF p.8
Notes: Stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, and lesser horn of the hyoid are second pharyngeal arch (Reichert cartilage) derivatives (Rodriguez-Vazquez, Morphogenesis of Reichert's Cartilage, J Anat 2006; de Bakker, Sci Rep 2019). Cross-system head/neck embryology with low cardiology relevance - reserve for embryology content. The ligament is not bone, so 'hyoid-associated structures' does not fully capture the set.

Explanation: The source lists these as cardiovascular adaptations contributing to improved athletic oxygen delivery and exercise performance.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Endurance training adaptations; Athlete cardiovascular physiology
Source Section: Exercise Physiology / Athletic Cardiovascular Physiology, PDF p.82
Notes: Increased stroke volume, higher VO2max, expanded plasma volume, and lower resting HR are endurance-training adaptations (Hellsten & Nyberg, Cardiovascular Adaptations to Exercise Training, Compr Physiol 2015). Responses vary with training type and individual; title is appropriately scoped to endurance training.

Explanation: The source describes sympathetic cardiac stimulation and enhanced venous return alongside vasodilation in active skeletal muscle.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Dynamic exercise hemodynamics; Aerobic exercise cardiovascular responses
Source Section: Exercise Physiology / Physiologic Changes, PDF p.80
Notes: Increased HR, increased contractility, increased venous return, and reduced systemic vascular resistance occur in dynamic/aerobic exercise (Hellsten & Nyberg, Compr Physiol 2015). Does not generalize to sustained isometric exercise; an AV fistula can mimic part of this low-resistance pattern - board overlap caution with CARD-002.

Connection Title: Aortic diseases that can lead to aortic regurgitation
Explanation: The source links these conditions to aortic dilation or structural disruption that can impair aortic valve closure.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Aortic-root causes of AR; Aortic causes of aortic insufficiency
Source Section: Valvular Disease / Aortic Dilatation, PDF p.149; Aortic Disease / Marfan, PDF p.143
Notes: Aortic dissection, thoracic aortic aneurysm, Marfan root dilation, and tertiary (syphilitic) aortitis can disrupt the root/valve apparatus -> AR (Choudhry & Etchells, JAMA 1999; Loeys, revised Ghent nosology, J Med Genet 2010). Location matters - distal disease may spare the valve. 'Thoracic aortic disease' is an acceptable related alias.

Connection Title: Agents associated with cardiomyopathic LV dysfunction
Explanation: The source identifies these anticancer agents and alcohol as exposures associated with cardiomyopathy or cardiotoxic ventricular dysfunction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cardiotoxic exposures; Agents associated with systolic cardiac dysfunction
Source Section: Cardiomyopathy / Additional Causes, PDF p.128; Other Causes, PDF p.136
Notes: Doxorubicin and daunorubicin (anthracyclines), trastuzumab (HER2 inhibitor, usually reversible type II), and chronic alcohol cause cardiomyopathy/LV dysfunction (Bozkurt, Circulation 2016; Chang, Cardiovascular Complications of Cancer Therapy, JACC 2017). 'Agents/exposures' framing is needed (alcohol is not an anticancer drug). Board overlap: shares doxorubicin and alcohol with CARD-011, and doxorubicin+daunorubicin are both anthracyclines - avoid placing with CARD-011 on one board.
